evidence: The encrypted storage core is real and well built. src/Forge.Infrastructure/Persistence/ForgeDbContext.cs discovers mappings from IEntityTypeConfiguration and applies a central soft-delete filter (lines 49-66); Directory.Packages.props pins Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite.Core plus SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlcipher 2.1.11 with a comment recording the plaintext-shipping incident; tests/Forge.Infrastructure.Tests/Persistence/DatabaseEncryptionTests.cs proves encryption by inspecting bytes on disk rather than trusting the library. 47 HasIndex declarations across 11 configuration files cover the hot query shapes. src/Forge.Core/Abstractions/Data/ holds a clean, EF-free repository and session abstraction that 13 app services use.
gaps: Three whole areas are missing or inert. (1) F04.05 - corruption detection and recovery - has no scheduled integrity cadence, no safety-copy service and no operation journal; grep for 'quick_check|OperationJournal|SafetyCopy|abnormal' over src/ returns one hit, the startup integrity_check. (2) Scale is not addressed anywhere: no 50,000-set or 100,000-food fixture exists in tests/, no QueryPlanTests.cs exists, and IRepository<T> exposes no query surface at all - ListAsync materialises the entire table, so the food catalogue is loaded in full on every keystroke. (3) The epic's own performance premise is contradicted by its own documentation: docs/security/database-encryption.md:37-41 records 469 ms per connection open under the passphrase key form Forge uses, against S04.01.01 AC1's 50 ms budget, and Forge opens a context per operation. evidence: The biometric app lock is real, reachable and unusually well reasoned. src/Forge.Core/Abstractions/Security/AppLockPolicy.cs is a pure decision function over an explicit input record, covering launch, grace period, the workout allowance and a backwards wall clock; docs/security/app-lock-threat-model.md records why each lifecycle event was chosen; src/Forge.App/Features/Security/AppLockLifecycleEvents.cs wires it through a LifecycleEventRegistration resolved from the container, so it is genuinely connected rather than dead code; and five test files under tests/Forge.Core.Tests/Security exercise the rules. The honesty requirements are met in full: the lock screen and settings screen both say plainly that this is a presentation gate, that it creates no online account, and that nothing is deleted on failure.
gaps: The feature promises 'enable, unlock, lock out and recover' - the Forge-owned lockout and recovery half does not exist. There is no PIN anywhere in the product: no six-digit setup, no confirmation, no five-attempt counter, no 60-second lockout, no forgotten-PIN recovery copy. The design delegates entirely to the platform prompt and its device-credential fallback, which is arguably the better answer and is described in docs/security/app-lock-threat-model.md, but no ADR records the substitution and every 'PIN' reference in the stories now means the device passcode rather than a Forge secret.

evidence: REQ2 is met verbatim in two places: src/Forge.App/Features/Security/ViewModels/AppLockPageViewModel.cs:30-40 and AppLockSettingsPageViewModel.cs:102-121 both state that the lock protects local app access, that anyone with the device passcode can pass it, and that no online account is involved. REQ3 is met by design and is documented on the abstraction itself - src/Forge.Core/Abstractions/Security/IAppLockAuthenticator.cs:7-12 records that Forge never sees, stores or derives anything from the credential and that the database key is not derived from it, so a failed prompt cannot make data unreadable. REQ5 is met and is the best part of the story: AppLockPolicy.cs:101-104 returns DisableBecauseUnavailable ahead of every other rule, and AppLockCoordinator.UnlockAsync:171-185 acts on it by switching the setting off and letting the user in, with an in-file comment explaining that staying locked would turn Forge into 'a vault with the key thrown away'. AC1 is met: AppLockCoordinator.TryEnableAsync requires one successful platform prompt before the setting changes. AC3 is met: platform lockout and cancellation map to LockedOut and Cancelled results (PlatformAppLockAuthenticator.cs) and the settings and lock screens both carry recovery copy stating nothing is deleted.
gaps: REQ1 and AC2 are unmet as written because there is no separate biometric toggle to gate. The app lock is a single on/off setting backed by the platform prompt, so it is offered whenever the device has any credential, not only when enrolled biometrics exist. AppLockSettingsPageViewModel.cs reports the capability honestly ('No fingerprint or face is enrolled, so Forge will ask for your PIN, pattern or passcode'), which is arguably a better answer than disabling a biometric-only switch, but the criterion's 'biometric lock is disabled with an explanation and PIN setup remains available' has no counterpart in the code: there is no Forge PIN setup to remain available. REQ4 is satisfied only by the platform - the Android and iOS prompts are configured to fall back to the device credential themselves - not by any Forge PIN. AC1's 'one successful platform prompt' and the on-device behaviour behind it could not be executed here.

evidence: There is no PIN in Forge. A case-insensitive grep over src/ for 'PIN', 'passcode', 'FailedAttempt' and 'lockout' returns 40 matches and every single one refers to the device credential, not a Forge secret: PlatformAppLockAuthenticator's error strings ('use your PIN, pattern or password'), AppLockSettingsPageViewModel's capability copy, and comments. There is no PIN entry control in src/Forge.App/Features/Security/AppLockPage.xaml - the page has exactly one action, an Unlock button that invokes the platform prompt (lines 18-22). There is no failed-attempt counter anywhere: src/Forge.Core/Abstractions/Security/AppLockStateMachine.cs and AppLockState.cs have no attempt count and no lockout-until timestamp, and IAppLockSettings stores only IsEnabled, GraceDuration, RelaxDuringActivity and HideInAppSwitcher. Neither src/Forge.Infrastructure/Security nor a PIN hash store exists.
gaps: Every requirement is unmet as written: no six-digit PIN setup, no confirmation match, no five-attempt threshold, no 60-second lockout with a visible countdown, and no biometric-success counter reset. AC1, AC2 and AC3 all fail because the mechanism they describe does not exist. Two things are worth separating out. First, REQ3 and REQ5 are actually satisfied in spirit by the chosen design and are stated to the user - AppLockSettingsPageViewModel's RecoveryText and the lock screen's NoDataLossText both say Forge cannot reset anything and nothing is deleted, and there is no support bypass because there is no server. Second, the substitution is deliberate and is described in docs/security/app-lock-threat-model.md, which frames the lock as a presentation gate satisfied by 'fingerprint, face, or device PIN, pattern or passcode'. It is very likely the better product decision - a Forge-owned PIN would need its own storage, its own hashing and its own lockout, all to protect against a threat the device lock already covers. But it is a decision that replaces this story rather than implementing it, and it is recorded in a threat model rather than an ADR, so the backlog and the code should be reconciled explicitly.

evidence: REQ2 is met: src/Forge.App/Features/Security/AppLockPage.xaml renders only static text - a heading, a prompt description, an Unlock button and two explanatory cards - with no binding to a profile name, body metric, workout, food or notification. REQ4 is met on both halves: AppLockPolicy.cs:106-109 returns Lock unconditionally for AppLockTrigger.Launched, so unlock state never survives a process restart (AC3), and the idle interval is the configurable GraceDuration from IAppLockSettings with a fixed option list (AppLockSettings.GraceOptions). REQ5 is met: AppLockCoordinator.UnlockAsync:187-195 only leaves the locked state when stateMachine.ApplyAuthentication accepts the result, so a failure, a cancellation or an unavailable prompt all keep the lock in place, and AppLockStateMachineTests covers the transitions. REQ3 is met indirectly but genuinely: AppLockPresenter.OnShellNavigated (lines 148-158) re-asserts the lock screen over anything that navigates while the state is Locked, so a profile-switch navigation cannot land - which is what AC2 asks for. The app-switcher cover is handled separately and correctly, held until the lock screen is actually on screen rather than merely decided (AppLockPresenter.cs:91-96).
gaps: REQ1 and AC1's 500 ms bound cannot be settled by reading and are excluded rather than credited - the code paths look right (iOS OnResignActivation applies the cover before the snapshot, per docs/security/app-lock-threat-model.md), but the timing needs a device. One genuine gap: AC2's 'no profile-switch command executes' is satisfied by re-navigation rather than by refusal. AppLockPresenter navigates back over whatever appeared, so a command that had already begun executing would still run - there is no guard inside ProfileSwitcherViewModel.SwitchToAsync or any other command that checks AppLockState before acting. In practice the lock page is the current page so the switcher is unreachable, but the invariant is positional rather than enforced. Also worth noting for the reader: the story's named artefact src/Forge.App/App.xaml.cs is not where any of this lives - the lifecycle hooks are registered from the Security feature's own folder via LifecycleEventRegistration, which is a better arrangement than the backlog assumed.

evidence: The negative half of this feature holds and is verifiable. No sign-in or social-login action appears anywhere in src/ - a search of the onboarding, profile and settings surfaces finds no credential field, Directory.Packages.props references no OAuth or authentication provider package, and ForgeRoutes.cs declares no sign-in or WebAuthenticator route. Every profile already carries a stable, immutable, time-ordered identifier (Entity.Id, Guid v7), which is the localProfileId half of the seam. docs/adr/0001-local-first-no-backend.md:22-26 records the decision that 'login/sign-up' is realised as an optional app lock rather than a local credential store.
gaps: The forward-compatibility seam the feature is named for does not exist in code. UserProfile has no externalIdentityId or equivalent nullable field, there is no AccountAttach route and no feature flag to disable, and no migration or test demonstrates attaching an identity without changing profile-owned row counts. ADR-0001:65 states that 'identity is modelled as a seam an account can later attach to' - as of this reconciliation that sentence describes an intention rather than the schema.

REQ5 is trivially met in that nothing requires a network identifier.
gaps: REQ1's second half is unmet: src/Forge.Domain/Profile/UserProfile.cs declares DisplayName, Kind, LastActivatedUtc, DateOfBirth, BiologicalSex, Height, ExperienceLevel, Goal, TargetWeight, GoalTimeframeWeeks, TargetDailyCalories, AvailableEquipment, MovementLimitations and TrainingDaysPerWeek - there is no externalIdentityId or any nullable remote-identity column, and a grep over src/ for ExternalIdentityId returns nothing. The Profile EF configuration and all three migrations confirm the column does not exist. REQ2 and REQ4 are unmet: src/Forge.App/Navigation/ForgeRoutes.cs declares 46 routes and none is AccountAttach, there is no feature-flag mechanism in the codebase at all, and consequently AC3's 'navigation returns a disabled-route result' has nothing to exercise - ShellNavigationService performs no route validation, so an unregistered route would surface as a raw MAUI navigation failure rather than a typed disabled-route result. evidence: Parts of the required documentation exist and are good. docs/adr/0001-local-first-no-backend.md:22-26 states the decision that what the brief called login/sign-up is realised as an optional app lock protecting on-device data, and that credential-based sign-up against a local store 'would be security theatre' - which covers REQ4's distinction between app lock and remote identity, and is reinforced at length by docs/security/app-lock-threat-model.md:14-28, which states the lock 'does not derive a key, hold a key, re-key anything, or add a second encryption layer' and is a presentation gate rather than encryption. Line 63-66 of the ADR states the forward-compatibility intent: stable identifiers and timestamps on every entity from the start, and identity modelled as an attachable seam. AC3 is met and checkable: no OAuth provider package appears in Directory.Packages.props, and no WebAuthenticator or sign-in route is registered in ForgeRoutes.cs or any feature registration.
gaps: Three of the five requirements have no documentation anywhere. REQ1 is unmet: no document in docs/ mentions Sign in with Apple or any equivalent privacy-preserving option, so AC1 has nothing to review - this matters commercially, because Apple's guideline 4.8 requires it once any third-party login ships. REQ3 is unmet: no document describes attaching an identity to the local profile id, and there is no migration test demonstrating unchanged profile-owned row counts, so AC2 cannot be run - there is no externalIdentityId to attach to (see S05.06.01). REQ5 is unmet: no document covers the delete and export consequences of a future remote identity. REQ2 is only half covered - the ADR says local credentials would protect nothing, but nothing states that a future social sign-in authenticates to a backend rather than protecting local data. This is a documentation story with a real deliverable, and the deliverable is roughly 40 percent written.

evidence: The safety layer is genuinely delivered and is the best work in this epic. src/Forge.Domain/Profile/GoalSafetyEvaluator.cs enforces a 1.0 percent weekly body-weight change cap, a BMI 18.5 floor and sex-specific daily calorie floors with cited public-health sources, all configurable through GoalSafetyOptions; src/Forge.Domain/Onboarding/GoalSafetyNarrator.cs turns the result into non-diagnostic copy that surfaces every objecting guardrail rather than only the first, and is called live from GoalWizardViewModel.cs:382 and :503, with ProfileStore.SaveSetupAsync refusing to write a refused goal. Measurement is properly modelled: Mass, Length and Percentage are value types stored canonically with explicit precision, and unit display is a separate preference layer (UnitPreferences, UnitFormatter).
gaps: The rest of the epic is mostly collected-but-unused data. Body metrics cannot be added, edited or deleted anywhere outside the six-step onboarding wizard - Profile is read-only and the Insights 'Add body metric' button navigates to a screen with no entry affordance. EnergyExpenditureCalculator implements Mifflin-St Jeor correctly and is unit-tested, and has zero callers in src/. ExerciseFilter.FromDeclaredInjuries likewise has zero callers. UserProfile.MovementLimitations and UserProfile.ExperienceLevel are both persisted and never used to shape a recommendation. Goals are a single enum, not up to three ranked goals. Limitations are free text, not structured body area / pattern / severity. Nothing filters exercises by declared equipment or contraindication. Avatars, progress photos and the photo privacy overlay do not exist at all, so F06.05 is entirely unimplemented.

evidence: Canonical storage is done properly: src/Forge.Domain/Measurement and src/Forge.Domain/Profile model Mass, Length and Percentage as value types, and src/Forge.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configurations/Training/TrainingConfigurations.cs:107-110 shows the pattern - store canonical metric with HasPrecision and a unit-named column. src/Forge.Core/Abstractions/Preferences/UnitPreferences.cs and UnitFormatter.cs supply a clean metric/imperial display layer that never touches the stored value. Body metrics are read back and charted: InsightsDataService.LoadBodyMetricsAsync builds a smoothed trend from the profile's own rows.
gaps: The feature outcome is 'users can update body metrics locally and understand how Forge derived any energy estimate', and neither half holds. There is no metric entry, edit or delete surface: ProfilePage.xaml contains no editable numeric control at all and BodyMetricsViewModel.AddBodyMetricAsync navigates to the Profile tab, which has none either. And no energy estimate is ever shown - EnergyExpenditureCalculator has no caller, ActivityLevel is on no entity, and BMI is computed only inside GoalSafetyEvaluator to refuse a target, never displayed. A third gap was confirmed by follow-up audit: the metric/imperial display layer is well built but almost unreached. Only Features/Profile/ProfileViewModel.cs and Features/Settings/ViewModels/UnitsSettingsPageViewModel.cs consume IUnitFormatter, against 48 hard-coded 'kg'/'cm'/'kcal'/'km' strings across 19 files in src/Forge.App, so selecting imperial changes the profile screen and nothing else. See S06.01.02.

evidence: Canonical storage is met. src/Forge.Domain/Profile/BodyMetric.cs stores a Mass, and Length/Mass are decimal-backed value types converted at the mapping boundary, so no float drift is possible - the pattern is visible at TrainingConfigurations.cs:107-110 (canonical kilograms, HasPrecision(10,3), LoadKilograms column name, with a comment explaining a float column could not represent a 0.25 kg increment). evidence: REQ1 is met: src/Forge.Core/Abstractions/Preferences/UnitPreferences.cs:6-12 declares MeasurementSystemPreference with Metric and Imperial, persisted under forge.preferences.units.system with Metric as the default. evidence: There is no metric history management surface. src/Forge.App/Features/Insights/ViewModels/BodyMetricsViewModel.cs builds a read-only trend from InsightsDataService.LoadBodyMetricsAsync and exposes exactly one command - AddBodyMetricAsync at line 111-112, which is Shell.Current.GoToAsync(ForgeRoutes.Profile). evidence: The guardrail engine is complete and live. src/Forge.Domain/Profile/GoalSafetyEvaluator.cs:34-95 evaluates weekly rate of change, daily energy floor and target BMI, each producing a typed SafetyAdvisory with a plain-language message and an optional support signpost; GoalSafetyOptions carries the thresholds as configurable values with their public-health sources cited in comments. src/Forge.Domain/Onboarding/GoalSafetyNarrator.cs surfaces every objecting guardrail rather than only the first, with an explicit reassurance that nothing was discarded. evidence: Goals are singular in both the domain and the UI. src/Forge.Domain/Profile/UserProfile.cs:43 declares one FitnessGoal property with no collection, no rank and no join entity; src/Forge.Infrastructure/Persistence/Configurations/Profile/ProfileConfigurations.cs maps it as a single column and none of the three migrations adds a goals table. src/Forge.App/Features/Profile/ProfileLabels.cs:16-17 offers five mutually exclusive labels - Lose weight, Maintain, Gain weight, Build strength, Improve fitness - bound to a single-selection dx:ComboBoxEdit in GoalWizardPage.xaml, and GoalWizardViewModel.cs:559 parses exactly one back. evidence: Three of the five requirements are implemented precisely and are reachable. evidence: Nothing implements an impact summary. evidence: The feature outcome is 'contraindicated exercises are excluded or clearly warned wherever recommendations and search results appear', and nothing in the product excludes or warns. evidence: The named location src/Forge.Domain/Profile/Limitations does not exist and neither does src/Forge.App/Features/Profile/Limitations.
